title: India Sent an Entire Field Hospital to Venezuela. It Got There Before Most of the World's Aid Did.
excerpt: Two IAF C-17s carried 35 tonnes of relief supplies, medicines and BHISHM Cubes to earthquake-ravaged La Guaira under 'Operation Amistad' — India's fastest disaster-response deployment to the Western Hemisphere in a decade.
body:
When twin earthquakes of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 tore through Venezuela's northern coast on Wednesday, the international rescue effort that followed became one of the largest in Latin American history. More than 900 people were killed, over 50,000 remain unaccounted for, and the United Nations estimates nearly seven million people could be affected, with direct damage close to $6.7 billion.

India's response was swift and unmistakable.

External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar announced that India had launched **Operation Amistad** — the Spanish word for friendship — dispatching two Indian Air Force C-17 Globemaster III aircraft loaded with an Indian Army Field Hospital Unit and more than 35 tonnes of relief supplies, medicines and medical equipment.

Among the most significant items in the cargo were two **BHISHM Cubes** — Bharat Health Initiative for Sahyog, Hita and Maitri — portable emergency medical units designed to provide rapid trauma care in disaster zones. Each cube is a self-contained system capable of treating up to 200 casualties, with built-in surgical kits, ventilators, oxygen concentrators and blood-processing equipment.

"India is committed to support the Government and people of Venezuela in this difficult time," Jaishankar said on X.

## The Scale of the Disaster

The earthquakes struck within minutes of each other on Wednesday, devastating the coastal state of La Guaira and the capital Caracas. At least 100 buildings — many of them residential high-rises — were destroyed or damaged in La Guaira, a popular beachside area.

Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodriguez said on Saturday that 1,600 members of foreign rescue teams had arrived, with 10 more countries still expected to join. Fourteen thousand military and police personnel are now deployed in La Guaira.

The U.S. Geological Survey estimates the final death toll could exceed 10,000, which would make it one of Latin America's deadliest earthquakes in a century.

Residents and volunteers have for days worked with limited equipment, sometimes digging with their hands. Looting has been reported at several sites. The country's already fragile power grid — crippled by years of underinvestment — remains largely down in affected areas, with only 60 percent of electricity restored elsewhere.

## India's Growing Disaster Diplomacy

Operation Amistad is not India's first major disaster-relief deployment, but it is among the fastest to the Western Hemisphere. India has previously sent aid following earthquakes in Nepal (2015), Turkey (2023) and Morocco (2023), as well as during the COVID-19 pandemic when it supplied vaccines to over 100 countries under the Vaccine Maitri initiative.

The deployment of BHISHM Cubes — developed by India's Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) — marks a relatively new addition to India's disaster-response toolkit. The cubes were first showcased at scale during the G20 summit India hosted in 2023, and their deployment to Venezuela represents one of the most high-profile international uses of the technology.

India joins a broad international coalition. El Salvador has sent 300 rescue workers, Spain deployed 57 soldiers and 40 firefighters, Germany sent two rescue teams with sniffer dogs, and the United States has committed over $150 million in aid and deployed a two-star general to coordinate relief.

## Why This Matters for the Diaspora

For the Indian diaspora, Operation Amistad carries significance beyond the immediate humanitarian response. An estimated 5,000 to 8,000 people of Indian origin live in Venezuela, primarily in Caracas, with many working in the oil, retail and pharmaceutical sectors. While no Indian casualties have been confirmed, the Indian Embassy in Caracas has activated an emergency helpline.

More broadly, the rapid deployment signals India's expanding capacity to project soft power across regions where its footprint has historically been modest. Latin America and the Caribbean host over one million people of Indian origin, and India's disaster-response capabilities are increasingly being watched as a measure of the country's global standing.

The operation also comes at a diplomatically complex moment. India is simultaneously managing tensions with the United States over the deaths of three Indian seafarers in the Strait of Hormuz, negotiating the final terms of its bilateral trade agreement with Washington, and deepening its strategic partnership with Europe through Prime Minister Modi's recent five-nation tour.

That India can sustain a humanitarian operation of this scale while navigating these competing pressures is itself a statement. Whether measured in tonnes of relief supplies or the speed of deployment, Operation Amistad is being read — in New Delhi and abroad — as a signal that India intends to be counted among the world's first responders, not just its largest democracies.
